96: That was the Amazon Prime Original movie starring Chris Pine and Thandiwe Newton, All the Old Knives.
97: Moving back and forth between the restaurant conversation and memories of Vienna eight years earlier, the film hides who is lying until the very end.
98: Although it initially looks like Henry is interrogating Celia, the structure that finally reveals both came to finish the other off is truly thrilling.
99: Chris Pine's final expression, calmly confessing everything until the end even while knowing the poison is spreading, lingers in your mind for a long time.
100: It is a quiet espionage film that builds tension solely through dialogue and facial expressions rather than action, making it even more intriguing if you keep the wine region, arsenic, and the old man's words in mind while watching.
101: Based on the 2015 novel of the same name by American author Olen Steinhauer, the screenplay was written by the author himself.
102: Befitting the creator of the drama series Berlin Station about the CIA's Berlin office, he captured the exact atmosphere inside an intelligence agency on screen.
103: The director is Denmark native Janus Metz, who made his name with the documentary Armadillo following Danish soldiers on the front lines in Afghanistan.
104: Perhaps because of that background, he creates suffocating tension purely through conversations in conference rooms and across dinner tables without a single gunfight.
105: Playing Henry, Chris Pine sets aside his usual hero persona to portray a man who lost everything trying to protect the one person most precious to him.
106: Thandiwe Newton's acting, shifting her gaze in an instant even while smiling and exchanging jokes, carries the film's tension all the way to the finish.
107: Station chief Vick is played by Laurence Fishburne, Morpheus from The Matrix, and knowing that this man of few words orchestrated the whole thing makes the opening scene look completely different.
108: The role of former deputy chief Bill was played by Jonathan Pryce, an Academy Award nominee for The Two Popes.
109: When you rewatch the film knowing the ending, the morning table joke about putting arsenic in the food and the remark about the wine region sound completely different.
110: Building quietly before erupting all at once in the final 20 minutes, this movie comes highly recommended if you prefer psychological warfare over flashy action.
